title: Shakalya's last question
hookLine: the last challenger argues to win, the warning that stopped Gargi comes true for him, and a riddle about a tree ends the debate
carry: the root of a person is knowing and joy
tomorrow: Janaka and Yajnavalkya: what is the light of man?
last: TRUTH IS ONE; THE WISE CALL IT MANY NAMES.

lines: HAVE THEY MADE YOU THEIR COAL-TONGS?
cards: After the countdown, Shakalya doesn't sit down. He keeps firing questions: the gods of each direction, what the heart rests on, what the self is founded on. Yajnavalkya answers each one.

Then, somewhere in the middle, he stops and asks Shakalya something. Shakalya, have these scholars made you their coal-tongs? Their tool for pulling hot coals out of the fire, so they don't burn their own hands?

teach.h: SENT IN TO WIN FOR THE OTHERS.
teach.b: That line tells you what's going on. Shakalya isn't Gargi, chasing a question to its edge. The others have sent him in to do the burning work for them, to win.
And he keeps going. So at last Yajnavalkya turns the debate around. Now I ask you, he says, about the person taught in the Upanishads.
If you can't tell me who he is, your head will fall off.

teach.h: HE DIDN'T KNOW, AND HIS HEAD FELL.
teach.b: Shakalya didn't know. And his head fell off: the text tells it in one plain sentence. Some readers take it literally, as the real stake of these Vedic debates; others hear an image: his whole argument came apart.
Either way, set it beside Gargi. She got the same warning, stopped, and came back with better questions. Then Yajnavalkya asks the room one last riddle.
A person is like a tree: hair for leaves, skin for bark, bones for the wood inside. Cut a tree down, and it grows again from the root.

teach.h: FROM WHAT ROOT DOES A PERSON GROW?
teach.b: When death cuts a person down, from what root does he grow? Nobody in the room dares take him on.
The chapter closes on its answer: Brahman, which is knowing, which is joy. That's the teaching.

teach.h: THE ROOT OF A PERSON IS KNOWING AND JOY.
teach.b: Under everything you are, there's a root no argument and no death can cut, and it isn't dull or blank: it is awareness, and it is joy.

Later Vedanta teachers gather this into a well-known name for Brahman: sat-chit-ananda, being, awareness, joy. Shakalya staked his head on winning. The Upanishad says your root was never in the winning.
Lose the argument, lose the job, lose someone you love: you've been cut down, not uprooted.

how: The Vedic brahmodya, a formal contest of questions about Brahman, is the setting of this chapter; teachers of the Upanishads read Shakalya's end alongside Gargi's warning, and the closing tree verses end the third book with a riddle.

s: Gargi's head falls off in the debate
she was warned, stopped, and came back with better questions. it's Shakalya whose head falls.
the tree riddle's answer is Brahman, which is knowing, which is joy
cut down by death, a person grows from that root, the text says.
the text explains what the head falling means
it says it in one plain line and moves on; readers take it literally or as an image.

games.q: Yajnavalkya asks the room: a tree cut down grows again from its root. a person cut down by death, from what root? nobody dares answer. what does the text say?
o: nothing; a person is simply gone.
Brahman, which is knowing, which is joy.
the family name, carried on by the children.
games.why: vijnanam anandam brahma: Brahman, knowing and joy. later Vedanta calls Brahman sat-chit-ananda: being, awareness, joy.

practice: Picture yourself as a tree: hair like leaves, skin like bark, bones like the hard wood inside, the body's weight settling like roots into soil.
Ask the old riddle, from what root do I grow, and let the text's answer rest in the body, not the head: knowing, and joy. If you pray, offer your prayer to that root; if not, simply rest there.

wordCard.voice: Murdha, the head. Shakalya staked his on winning, and lost it. The root, the text says, was never in the stakes.

orig.note: Sanskrit mūrdhan (nominative mūrdhā): the head, the top. the stake in the Brihadaranyaka's debates.

carryVoice: Your line: the root of a person is knowing and joy. Gargi asked to know; Shakalya argued to win. Day three hundred eighty-one, done.
